title: What does their move want? Surviving the early queen

difficulty.label: On-ramp opponent-intent series #1: every White move here wants something specific

objective.summary: Before every reply, answer two questions out loud: what does their move WANT, and what is the piece that just moved NO LONGER doing? This drill is the most common attack a 1000-1400 player ever faces — the early queen against f7 — and every defensive move in it is found by answering those two questions, never by memory.

planClasses.label: It aims at f7 — the mate address
planClasses.description: The move adds an attacker to f7, the one square only your king defends. Test: count the attackers pointing at f7 and ask whether Qxf7 next move would be mate or nonsense. If two pieces aim there, defending f7 outranks everything else on the board.

planClasses.label: It attacks something of yours that is loose
planClasses.description: The move attacks a pawn or piece with more attackers than defenders. Test: name the target, count both sides on that square, and prefer the defence that also develops a piece.

planClasses.label: It develops — no immediate demand
planClasses.description: The move improves a piece without threatening anything you can lose this move. Your licence to continue your own plan: develop, prepare to castle, take the centre.

planClasses.label: The moved piece left a job behind
planClasses.description: Whatever a piece moves toward, it also moves AWAY from something: a pawn it defended, a square it covered, a file it blocked. Test: look at the square the piece came from and name one thing it was doing there that nobody does now.

annotations: Your centre answer — and the drill's premise: you played a normal move, and White is about to stop playing normal moves. From here on, read every White move with the two questions before you touch a piece.

Question one: what does it want? The queen attacks e5 — count it: attacked once, defended by nobody — and she is sitting on the diagonal toward f7. Question two: what did she stop doing? Guarding d-file squares back home. The immediate bill is e5; pay it with a move that develops.

The answer both questions point to: the knight defends e5 from its best square and develops. You did not retreat, you did not push a panicked pawn — you answered the threat with a move you wanted anyway. The attacker has spent a queen move; you have spent nothing.

Question one again — and this time the answer is mate: bishop and queen both aim at f7, and Qxf7 next move would be the end. Everything else on the board, including your own plans, is now irrelevant for exactly one move.

The blocking answer with a bonus: g6 closes the h5-f7 diagonal AND attacks the queen, so she must spend another move. Two queen moves for one pawn move — you are winning the only race the opening runs, and the mate is off.

Both questions in one move. What does it want? Mate on f7 again, now down the f-file with the bishop still supporting. What did she stop doing? Attacking e5 — the threat you paid for two moves ago is gone, which is exactly why you must re-read the position instead of remembering it.

Same method, third verse: the knight blocks the f-file at f6, develops, and prepares castling. Three White threats have now been answered by three Black developing moves. The attack is spent, and White's queen has personally donated the tempo count that decides the next ten moves.

checkpoints.label: Qh5 — read it before you touch a piece
Bc4 — count the attackers on f7 now
Qf3 — what does it want, what did it abandon?
Three threats read, three developing answers

deviations.note: The right move one position too early — it answers the f7 idea and ignores what the move ACTUALLY wants right now: e5. 3.Qxe5+ takes the pawn with check and forks the h8 rook through the hole g6 just opened. Read the move in front of you, not the move you were warned about.

Developing with an attack on the queen — the right instinct, wrong order: it leaves e5 hanging, and 3.Qxe5+ collects the pawn with check before the knight's attack matters. Threats outrank attacks: answer what their move wants first, then hit back. Engine pass 2026-08-15 (Stockfish 18, depth 22): the pawn is real (material 39-38 after 3.Qxe5+) but the position is not — 2...Nf6 costs 0.20 against the spine's 2...Nc6, and 3.Qxe5+ Be7 evaluates at -0.18. This class asserts a tactical error whose measured cost is far below this pack's own 150-centipawn guard, so the guard will not fire on it.
Defending e5 with the pawn works and frees the c8 bishop. It develops nothing, so the spine prefers ...Nc6 — but this is a sound answer to the same correctly-read threat.

The queen defends e5 and shields e-file tricks — a correct reading paid for at the wrong counter: your queen now blocks the f8 bishop, and you have answered one developed attacker by undeveloping yourself. Play it out and compare the move-8 positions with the ...Nc6 line.

The classic Scholar's Mate victim: a good developing move that answers yesterday's question. Two pieces aim at f7 and the knight defends none of it — 4.Qxf7# ends the game. When the answer to 'what does it want' is MATE, development goes to the back of the queue.

A normal move that does not touch the f7 count: still two attackers, still one defender, still 4.Qxf7#. The point of this branch is painful and permanent — normal moves lose instantly when a mate threat is on the board unanswered.

The queen covers f7 from e7 — a correct defence that reads the threat right. Its price is the blocked f8 bishop; the spine's ...g6 defends while gaining a tempo on the queen instead. Both answers pass the reading test; one of them also wins time.

Covering f7 by copying White's crime — your own early queen. It holds the mate and offers to trade the attack away, but the queen stands on the knight's square and White develops against her with tempo. A readable defence with a built-in tax; branch it and compare.

The move LOOKS ferocious — the knight attacks the queen and forks toward c2 — and it loses to the one thing it does not do: 5.Qxf7#. Attacking their queen is not an answer to their mate. This branch is the whole pack in one move: threats outrank attacks, every time.

The right IDEA — cut the c4 bishop's support of f7 — priced at a pawn: both exd5 and Bxd5 keep the pressure and win material, because the d5 block itself can be captured. Compare with ...Nf6, which blocks a line nothing can capture on. Blocks are only as good as their squares.

Offering the queen trade — the reading is correct (f7 covered) and the offer is real: a traded queen is a spent attack. Costs more than ...Nf6 (your queen developed early, his choice whether to trade) but passes both questions honestly.

The same steady defence as one move earlier: f7 covered from e7. Solid, passive, and it keeps failing to punish the queen for her travels — which is why the spine's ...Nf6 (defend, develop, prepare castling) is the model answer.

feedbackClaims.text: Two questions before every reply: what does their move want, and what is the piece that just moved no longer doing? The first finds their threat; the second finds your opportunity. At 1000-1400, games are decided by whoever forgets to ask the first question — the second is how you start winning them.

A threat you can execute next move outranks an attack on any piece, including the queen. The ...Nd4 branch exists to make this permanent: the knight attacks her majesty herself and White simply plays mate. Check what they can DO to you before admiring what you can do to them.

Each time the early queen is met by a developing defence or hit by a pawn with tempo, the defender banks a free move. Over the three readings in this pack White spends three queen moves on an attack that ends with Black better developed — the standard fate of the early queen against a defender who counts.

This pack's guard is set tighter than the principles packs (150 centipawns) on purpose: here every wrong move IS a misread threat, and its cost — a pawn with check, a fork, mate — should arrive within a ply or two so the misread and the consequence are still in the same breath. Nothing quieter than a misread can trip it.

sources: Line identity: 2.Qh5 against 1.e4 e5 (Danvers/Wayward Queen family) and the Scholar's-mate pattern via Bc4+Qf3; the drilled defence ...Nc6/...g6/...Nf6 is the standard refutation scheme. No theory beyond move identity is claimed; the pack drills the READING method (the owner's two questions from design/00-thesis.md §Target player), not the line.

MECHANICAL: every spine move and every deviation move replayed legal with chessops this session; `make pack-check` independently re-walks spine and deviations. The three mate branches were replayed to the mating position: after 3...Nf6 4.Qxf7# and 3...d6 4.Qxf7# and 4...Nd4 5.Qxf7# the mate is rules-checkable (king attacked by the f7 queen supported by the c4 bishop; d7/e7 covered along the seventh rank, d8 occupied by Black's own queen, f8 by the bishop, Kxf7 illegal). The Qxe5+ fork geometry after 2...g6 (e5 to h8 clear through f6/g7) was replayed legal on the derived position.

MECHANICAL: the intent answers the annotations assert are attack-count arithmetic on the derived FENs (f7 attacker/defender counts; the e5 attack existing after Qh5 and not after Qf3). The runtime's direct_attack_count vocabulary could express these counts; this draft states them in prose only.

UNGROUNDED: every strategic judgment — plan-class prose, annotations, deviation classifications and notes, feedbackClaims, and every 'model answer' ranking among the sound defences (...Nc6 over ...d6/...Qe7, ...g6 over ...Qe7, ...Nf6 over the queen moves) — is agent-authored with NO citation and NO human review, and — after the 2026-08-15 engine pass — with evaluated MOVES but still unevaluated PROSE.

ENGINE PASS (mechanical, 2026-08-15): Stockfish 18 at the repo's authoring profile — depth 22, Threads 1, Hash 16MB, MultiPV 1 — run through apps/server's EngineSupervisor and StockfishEvidenceExecutor, the same engine path make candidate-emit --engine-eval uses. 7 decision positions and 20 candidate moves were evaluated: every spine node's resulting position, every authored deviation's resulting position, and the engine's own depth-22 first choice at each decision. Per-move centipawns and losses are in provenance.engineValidation. Loss is candidate-relative (best evaluated candidate minus this move) and is therefore a LOWER BOUND: all legal moves were not enumerated. Spine moves the engine ranks materially below a sibling at the same position: Qh5 (w2-qh5) 0.75 below Nf3.
graduationBlockers: There is no pack review workflow in this system and there never will be one (owner ruling 2026-08-13). Only a citable source or mechanical validation that bears on a claim clears a blocker.

ENGINE-CHECKED 2026-08-15 and all three rankings are reproduced exactly at depth 22, in Black's favour throughout. After 2.Qh5: ...Nc6 +0.42 > ...d6 +0.37 > ...Qe7 +0.08. After 3.Bc4: ...g6 +0.37 > ...Qe7 +0.12 > ...Qf6 -0.21. After 4.Qf3: ...Nf6 +0.39 > ...Qe7 +0.19 > ...Qf6 +0.14. This is the strongest confirmation the pass produced anywhere in the opening corpus. The punishments are confirmed too: 2...g6 -4.60, and 3...Nf6, 3...d6 and 4...Nd4 all evaluate as forced mate for White. The one row the pass does NOT support is 2...Nf6, classed tactical_error at a measured cost of 0.20 — below this pack's own 150-centipawn guard, which therefore cannot fire on it. The class was left as authored and the contradiction recorded in the deviation note.
The 4...d5 note claims both exd5 and Bxd5 keep the attack and win material; only the LEGALITY of those captures was verified, not the evaluation or the follow-ups.

The intent_capture checkpoints have no format slot for the validated answer: the pack knows (by attack arithmetic) which plan class each White move serves, and can say so only in annotations. If the interaction ever grades intent, these claims need mechanical grounding via direct_attack_count expressions, which the format has but this draft does not yet encode.
The guard threshold (150cp) encodes an authored claim that every materially-costly move here is a misread; no play-test evidence supports the number.

ENGINE EVIDENCE NOW RECORDED — the root and authored positions have fixed-depth, manifest-linked Stockfish measurements. This makes the stated root assessment falsifiable at the named engine version and cost; it does not ground strategic prose, plan classes, annotations, or deviation classifications, and it is not a proof.

CORPUS-CHECKED 2026-08-15 and NOT ANSWERABLE from repo data: this pack targets the 1000-1400 band, but both shipped Lichess-explorer artifacts (content/candidates/priority/priority.json and content/candidates/priority-wave4a/priority.json) were pulled at ratings 1400/1600/1800 only. Every 'what players at this level actually play' claim in this pack therefore has no corpus behind it and cannot acquire one without a new explorer pull at the 1000/1200/1400 bands. The 2026-08-15 engine pass measured what the moves cost; it says nothing about how often they are played.
